title: Macbeth
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Eleventh-century Scotland, with one scene at the English court
lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines, the shortest of the major tragedies
openingLine: When shall we three meet again In thunder, lightning, or in rain?
summary: Three witches greet a victorious general with a prophecy that he will be king. Within a day he has murdered the king who trusts him, and the rest of the play watches him kill to keep a crown that gives him nothing. It is the shortest of Shakespeare’s tragedies and moves quickly: Macbeth is never given time to reconsider.
referenceStyle: act, scene and line of the Astor Library Edition

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Macbeth
sourceText.note: Other modern editions vary by a line or two. A few quotations follow the Astor Library Edition’s wording where this text reads differently.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The witches, and the plan to kill Duncan
structure.summary: Macbeth and Banquo meet the witches on the heath and hear that Macbeth will be thane of Cawdor and king. When the first title arrives within minutes, the second stops being an absurdity. Lady Macbeth reads his letter, judges him too decent to take the nearest way, and has the murder arranged before he reaches the door.

scenes.title: Thunder
scenes.summary: Three witches agree to meet Macbeth on the heath.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.summary: A wounded sergeant describes Macbeth carving his way through a rebel army.

scenes.title: The prophecy
scenes.summary: The witches hail Macbeth as Glamis, Cawdor and king hereafter, and tell Banquo he will father kings.

scenes.title: Malcolm named heir
scenes.summary: Duncan thanks Macbeth and then names his own son Prince of Cumberland, putting a step in Macbeth’s way.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth’s letter and calls on the spirits to strip her of pity.

scenes.title: The welcome
scenes.summary: Duncan arrives at Inverness and praises the sweetness of the air.

scenes.title: The argument
scenes.summary: Macbeth decides against the murder; his wife changes his mind in under fifty lines.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Duncan’s murder, and the knocking at the gate
structure.summary: Macbeth sees a dagger that is not there, kills Duncan offstage, and comes back unable to say ‘Amen’. The knocking at the gate, the Porter’s drunken joke about hell and the discovery of the body make a private act a public emergency. Malcolm and Donalbain run, which conveniently makes them suspects.

scenes.title: The dagger
scenes.summary: Banquo confesses uneasy dreams; alone, Macbeth follows a dagger he cannot grasp.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: Macbeth returns with the grooms’ daggers, hearing a voice cry sleep no more.

scenes.title: The knocking
scenes.summary: The Porter plays hell’s gatekeeper; Macduff discovers the body and Macbeth kills the grooms.

scenes.title: Unnatural signs
scenes.summary: Ross and an Old Man report horses eating each other; Macbeth goes to Scone to be crowned.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Banquo’s murder, and the banquet
structure.summary: Banquo suspects and says nothing. Macbeth, who now fears the second half of the prophecy more than the first, hires murderers without telling his wife. Fleance escapes, the ghost sits in Macbeth’s chair at the banquet, and the marriage that planned Duncan’s murder starts to come apart over Banquo’s.

scenes.title: Banquo's suspicion
scenes.summary: Banquo weighs what Macbeth has gained; Macbeth hires two murderers.

scenes.title: Scorpions
scenes.summary: Macbeth keeps his wife ignorant of the plan for the first time.

scenes.title: The ambush
scenes.summary: Banquo is killed and Fleance escapes into the dark.

scenes.title: The banquet
scenes.summary: Banquo’s ghost takes Macbeth’s seat and the state dinner collapses.

scenes.title: Hecate
scenes.summary: Hecate rebukes the witches, in a scene most scholars think was added later.

scenes.title: Rumour
scenes.summary: Lennox speaks in careful irony; Macduff has gone to England.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The apparitions, and the murder of Macduff’s family
structure.summary: Macbeth demands more prophecy and is given three riddles that sound like safety. He orders the killing of Macduff’s wife and children, an act with no strategic purpose at all. In England, Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be worse than the tyrant, and the news from home arrives.

scenes.title: The apparitions
scenes.summary: Beware Macduff; none of woman born shall harm Macbeth; he is safe till Birnam wood moves.

scenes.title: Fife
scenes.summary: Lady Macduff’s son is murdered on stage, and she is chased off crying murder.

scenes.title: The English court
scenes.summary: Malcolm tests Macduff’s loyalty; Ross brings the news from Fife.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The sleepwalking scene, and Macbeth’s death
structure.summary: Lady Macbeth washes hands that are clean. Macbeth, told of her death, can find no more feeling in it than a line about tomorrow. Birnam wood moves because the army carries it; the man not of woman born was delivered by caesarean section. Every guarantee holds and every one betrays him.

scenes.title: Sleepwalking
scenes.summary: A doctor and gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth relive the murders in her sleep.

scenes.title: The march
scenes.summary: The Scottish lords join Malcolm’s army near Birnam.

scenes.title: The yellow leaf
scenes.summary: Macbeth clings to the apparitions and asks the doctor to cure his wife’s mind.

scenes.title: Branches
scenes.summary: Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a bough for cover.

scenes.title: Tomorrow
scenes.summary: The queen is dead; a messenger reports that the wood is moving.

scenes.title: The assault
scenes.summary: The army throws down its screen of branches.

scenes.title: Young Siward
scenes.summary: Macbeth kills a man he cannot fear and begins to look for Macduff.

scenes.title: The end
scenes.summary: Macduff reveals his birth, kills Macbeth, and Malcolm is hailed king.

characters.name: Macbeth
characters.role: Thane of Glamis, then Cawdor, then king of Scotland
characters.summary: A soldier praised for a savagery the state approves of, who discovers that the same nerve is unbearable when he uses it for himself. He imagines every murder in full before he commits it and feels every consequence afterwards.
characters.clue: A soldier whose imagination is his conscience: he sees the dagger before he uses it and hears the voice that will not let him sleep afterwards.

relationships.label: married to
relationships.note: Partners in the first murder, strangers by the third.

characters.name: Lady Macbeth
characters.summary: She reads her husband accurately in a single speech and organises the murder he cannot organise himself. Her strength is a performance she has to summon, and once the crown is won she has no further part to play, which is where the sleepwalking begins.
characters.clue: She calls on spirits to unsex her, tells her husband to look like the innocent flower, and later cannot get a spot off a clean hand.

characters.name: Banquo
characters.summary: He hears the same prophecy and does nothing with it, which sets him against Macbeth from the start. His silence after Duncan’s death is not innocence either: he suspects Macbeth of foul play and keeps quiet because the prophecy also promised something to him.
characters.clue: Told that he will father kings though he will not be one, he is murdered on the road at dusk and comes back to sit in the king’s place at a feast.

characters.name: Duncan
characters.summary: Generous, trusting and a poor judge of faces: he says as much about the last thane of Cawdor moments before promoting the next traitor. Shakespeare makes him gentler than the historical king so that the murder costs the audience something.
characters.clue: He says there is no art to find the mind’s construction in the face, praises the sweet air at his host’s castle, and is murdered there that night.

characters.name: Macduff
characters.summary: He discovers the body, stays away from the coronation, and leaves for England without warning his household, a decision the play does not let him off. His grief in 4.3 is the one moment where a man is allowed to feel a loss fully before acting on it.
characters.clue: He finds his king murdered, stays away from the coronation at Scone, and was from his mother’s womb untimely ripped.

relationships.label: kills, in revenge for his family

characters.name: Malcolm
characters.role: Duncan’s elder son, Prince of Cumberland
characters.summary: Named heir in 1.4, which is the political fact that makes the prophecy inconvenient. He flees, learns caution, and sounds out Macduff by describing himself as a worse tyrant than Macbeth, a scene that shows a king being made.
characters.clue: He flees to England after his father’s murder, tests a loyal thane by slandering himself, and has his soldiers hew down boughs to carry before them.

characters.name: The Weird Sisters
characters.summary: They tell the truth in a form designed to be misheard. Nothing they say forces anybody to do anything, which is the difficulty: the play never settles whether they cause the future or only describe it accurately enough to be dangerous.
characters.clue: They meet in thunder on a heath, hail a soldier by three titles, and leave him sure he is safe until a wood comes to a hill.

characters.name: Lady Macduff
characters.summary: She gets one scene, and uses it to say the thing nobody else will: that a man who leaves his wife and children unguarded has behaved like a traitor to them, whatever his politics. Her son is killed in front of her, and she is chased off the stage crying ‘Murder!’.
characters.clue: She calls her absent husband a traitor to his family, tells her son she can buy twenty husbands at any market, and is murdered in her own castle.

characters.name: Fleance
characters.summary: He speaks only a few lines and then escapes into the dark, and the second half of the play runs on that escape. James VI and I was held to be descended from Banquo through Fleance.
characters.clue: He tells his father the moon is down, carries the torch on the road at dusk, and escapes into the dark when his father is killed.

themes.name: Ambition
themes.summary: The play is careful to show that ambition is not the same as wanting power. Macbeth has power already and is praised for it; what the witches give him is a way of picturing more, and the picture will not leave him alone. Shakespeare gives the desire a body (a spur, a leap, a fall) and no destination.
themes.development: Suggested in 1.3, argued over in 1.7, and by 3.4 it has become momentum: he is so far in blood that going back would be as tedious as going on.

themes.name: Guilt and conscience
themes.summary: Guilt in this play is physical. It stops a man saying ‘Amen’, it will not wash off, it takes a seat at dinner, and it eventually walks the corridors at night with a candle. Nobody is punished for the murders by the state; they are punished by their own minds and bodies.
themes.development: Macbeth’s imagination runs ahead of his conscience in Acts I and II, and his wife’s runs behind hers: she is unshaken at the murder and destroyed by it in Act V.

themes.name: Kingship and the state
themes.summary: Scotland is described as a body: bleeding, sick, needing a physician. Malcolm’s list of the king-becoming graces in 4.3 sets out what Macbeth is not, and the play’s interest is less in who deserves the crown than in what happens to a country when its head is afraid.
themes.development: Duncan’s Scotland rewards loyalty in public; Macbeth’s rewards silence; Malcolm’s begins with a promise of order that the audience has been given reason to doubt.

themes.name: Fate, prophecy and equivocation
themes.summary: Every prophecy in the play comes true, and the ones Macbeth relies on mislead him. The apparitions promise safety in terms that are technically exact and practically worthless, which is the same trick the Jesuit doctrine of equivocation was accused of in the Gunpowder Plot trials of 1606.
themes.development: The prophecies move from prediction to riddle: Birnam wood does move, and the man not of woman born does exist.

themes.name: Appearance and reality
themes.summary: The play opens by declaring that fair is foul, and then shows it again and again: a welcoming castle, a loyal host, an innocent flower, a safe prophecy. Characters repeatedly fail to read each other.
themes.development: Duncan cannot find the mind’s construction in the face; by Act IV Malcolm will not trust a face at all, and tests Macduff with a false one of his own.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: “When you durst do it, then you were a man” is an argument as much as an insult, and it works. The play returns again and again to what manhood is supposed to allow: Macduff’s answer in 4.3, that he must also feel the loss as a man, is offered as a correction to everything Macbeth has been told.
themes.development: Lady Macbeth asks to be unsexed in 1.5; Macbeth tells his wife to bring forth men-children only in 1.7; Macduff rejects the equation in 4.3.

techniques.name: Equivocation
techniques.definition: Saying something literally true in a form designed to be understood wrongly.
techniques.inThisBook: The witches’ apparitions and the Porter’s joke about the equivocator who could not equivocate to heaven belong to the same 1606 argument about oaths and mental reservation.

techniques.name: Blood imagery
techniques.definition: A repeated image used to bind separate scenes into one idea.
techniques.inThisBook: Blood arrives as heroism in 1.2, becomes a stain in 2.2, a debt in 3.4 and a hallucination in 5.1 without ever leaving the stage.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Macbeth’s soliloquies are where the murders actually happen; by Act V they have thinned to a report on how little he feels.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Balancing opposed terms against each other inside one line.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘Fair is foul, and foul is fair’ sets the pattern, and the play goes on pairing terms that ought to exclude each other: lost and won, innocent flower and serpent.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Duncan praising the sweetness of the air at Inverness is the clearest case: the audience has just heard what is waiting inside.

techniques.name: Disordered nature
techniques.definition: Weather and animal behaviour made to answer human action.
techniques.inThisBook: Horses eat each other, an owl kills a falcon and darkness strangles the day after Duncan’s murder: the killing of a king is reported as a fault in the world.

quotations.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair: / Hover through the fog and filthy air.
quotations.speaker: The Witches
quotations.context: The closing couplet of the first scene, spoken by all three witches together.
quotations.analysis: Twelve lines into the play, the audience is handed its instructions: nothing here will be safely readable. The chiasmus makes two opposed words a closed loop, and the shift into rhymed trochaic tetrameter sets the witches apart from every other voice in the play before they have done anything at all.

quotations.text: All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!
quotations.speaker: Third Witch
quotations.context: The third of three greetings on the heath, after Glamis and Cawdor.
quotations.analysis: The sentence does not contain an instruction, a condition or a route. It is the flat future tense that does the damage: Macbeth is told what will be, and spends the play converting a prediction into a plan while believing he is only keeping an appointment.

quotations.text: It is too full o' the milk of human kindness / To catch the nearest way.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Reading Macbeth’s letter about the prophecy, alone.
quotations.analysis: She diagnoses him in a single image, and the image is no insult: it grants him a nature she considers a practical obstacle. ‘The nearest way’ is the whole murder rendered as a route on a map, which is exactly the kind of euphemism the couple will need for the next two acts.

quotations.text: Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here, / And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full / Of direst cruelty!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, after learning that Duncan will arrive that night.
quotations.analysis: The cruelty she wants has to be sent for, which tells the audience she does not already possess it. ‘Crown to the toe’ puts the crown on her body as well as on Duncan’s head, and the request to be unsexed treats womanhood as a set of feelings (pity, remorse, the milk she later names) that would get in the way.

quotations.text: Look like the innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Instructing Macbeth as Duncan approaches the castle.
quotations.analysis: The advice is a compressed piece of stage direction: a face to wear and a thing to be. It also answers Duncan’s complaint sixty lines earlier that there is no art to find the mind’s construction in the face: here is the art, and it belongs to the other side.

quotations.text: If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well / It were done quickly.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, leaving the banquet at which Duncan is his guest.
quotations.analysis: Three uses of ‘done’ in fourteen words, and not one of them names the act. The line goes in circles because the speaker will not let the word ‘murder’ into it, and the soliloquy goes on to reject the plan on grounds of consequence more than conscience.

quotations.text: I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself / And falls on the other.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The end of the soliloquy in which he decides not to kill Duncan.
quotations.analysis: He can find no reason for the murder except the wanting of it, and he says so as though that settled the matter. The rider who over-leaps the saddle is a comic image for a catastrophic one, and the sentence breaks off before it lands, leaving the fall to the rest of the play.

quotations.text: Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand?
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at night, moving towards Duncan’s chamber.
quotations.analysis: The dagger is offered to him handle first, as a servant would offer it: the hallucination is helpfully arranging the murder. He asks a question, and goes on asking: the speech is a man running an experiment on his own mind, and losing.

quotations.text: Methought I heard a voice cry 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep'.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Immediately after the murder, still holding the daggers.
quotations.analysis: He reports the sentence without owning it, and the voice uses his name as though he were already a story being told about someone else. Sleep is the first of the ordinary things the murder takes away, and three acts later Lady Macbeth is walking in hers.

quotations.text: Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather / The multitudinous seas incarnadine, / Making the green one red.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Looking at his hands after Duncan’s murder.
quotations.analysis: The scale inverts inside four lines: an ocean cannot clean one hand, so the hand stains the ocean. ‘Incarnadine’ and ‘multitudinous’ are Latinate and enormous; ‘making the green one red’ is four monosyllables and a colour. Shakespeare gives the man the grand version and then the plain one, and the plain one is worse.

quotations.text: O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Speaking to Lady Macbeth while concealing the plan to kill Banquo.
quotations.analysis: The endearment and the scorpions arrive in the same breath, and he tells her about the state of his mind so as to avoid telling her its contents. This is the scene where the marriage stops being a partnership: from here he acts and she is informed afterwards, if at all.

quotations.text: It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: After the guests have been sent away from the ruined banquet.
quotations.analysis: He quotes a proverb, which is the closest he now comes to a moral framework: murder is described as a creature with an appetite of its own. The grammar has no agent in it anywhere: by Act III he has stopped experiencing his killings as things he decides to do.

quotations.text: Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be until / Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill / Shall come against him.
quotations.speaker: Third Apparition
quotations.context: The third apparition, a crowned child holding a tree.
quotations.analysis: The prophecy hands him an impossibility and he accepts the gift without examining the wrapping, though a child holding a branch has already shown him how the wood will move. Equivocation works here by offering a picture the listener would like to keep; nobody lies.

quotations.text: Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak / Whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break.
quotations.speaker: Malcolm
quotations.context: To Macduff, on hearing that his wife and children are dead.
quotations.analysis: This is the one piece of straightforwardly good advice in the play, and it is about language. Set it against Macbeth, who has spent four acts refusing to name what he is doing; the play’s cure for grief is the opposite of the habit that produced it.

quotations.text: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Sleepwalking, watched by a doctor and her gentlewoman.
quotations.analysis: She told her husband in 2.2 that a little water clears us of this deed, and she is now scrubbing a hand that has nothing on it. The speech is in prose, which for a queen at this point in a tragedy is itself a diagnosis, and it breaks into fragments that move between all three murders.

quotations.text: My way of life / Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf; / And that which should accompany old age, / As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, / I must not look to have.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at Dunsinane as the English army approaches.
quotations.analysis: He itemises exactly what he has lost, in order, and the list is entirely made of relationships. It is the most accurate self-assessment anyone makes in the play, and it changes nothing: within a few lines he is calling for his armour.

quotations.text: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, / Creeps in this petty pace from day to day / To the last syllable of recorded time.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: On being told that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: Asked to feel something about his wife’s death, he produces a theory of time instead. The repetition flattens the future into a queue, and ‘syllable’ reduces all of history to something merely said aloud, which sets up the walking shadow and the poor player five lines later.

quotations.text: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage / And then is heard no more.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is aimed at the actor saying it, in a theatre, to people who will go home in an hour. It is the bleakest thing in the play and also the most theatrically self-aware: the man who wanted to be remembered as king describes existence as a performance nobody will recall.

quotations.text: Macduff was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Macduff
quotations.context: In single combat with Macbeth, answering the claim that no man of woman born can harm him.
quotations.analysis: The last guarantee fails on a technicality, and the technicality is a birth. Macbeth’s answer, that the word has ‘cow’d my better part of man’, admits the whole trick: he had been fighting on the strength of a sentence more than an army.

quotations.text: Our fears do make us traitors.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macduff
quotations.context: To Ross, on learning that her husband has fled to England.
quotations.analysis: In six words she convicts Macduff of the thing the whole play is about: acting on fear and calling it strategy. She is defending nobody, least of all herself, and the scene that follows makes her the only character permitted to be simply right.

quotations.text: More needs she the divine than the physician.
quotations.speaker: Doctor
quotations.context: After watching Lady Macbeth sleepwalk.
quotations.analysis: Medicine hands the case over: what is wrong with her is not a condition. The line pairs with Macbeth’s demand two scenes later that the same doctor pluck a rooted sorrow from the memory, and with Scotland itself, repeatedly described as a patient nobody can treat.

quotations.text: Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Aside, immediately after Duncan names Malcolm his heir.
quotations.analysis: The first thing he does after the obstacle appears is ask the universe to look away. Light and dark run through the whole play as a moral lighting rig, and here Macbeth is operating it himself: he wants not to be seen, even by himself.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth becomes king of Alba
timeline.detail: He ruled for seventeen years, a reign Shakespeare compresses to a few violent months.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth is killed at Lumphanan
timeline.detail: Not at Dunsinane, and not by Macduff.

timeline.label: Holinshed’s Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare’s chief source for the Scottish material, including the meeting with the three weird sisters.

timeline.label: James VI publishes Daemonologie
timeline.detail: The future king of England writes a dialogue on witchcraft six years before inheriting the English throne.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A Scottish king in London, claiming descent from Banquo, changes what a Scottish play on a London stage can mean.

timeline.label: The Gunpowder Plot
timeline.detail: The conspiracy and its trials put the word equivocation into everyday London use.

timeline.label: Macbeth most likely written and first performed
timeline.detail: The Porter’s equivocator is the strongest internal evidence for the date.

timeline.label: Simon Forman records seeing Macbeth at the Globe
timeline.detail: The earliest surviving eyewitness account of the play in performance.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early printed text of the play, and a short one.

timeline.label: Verdi’s Macbeth premieres in Florence
timeline.detail: Revised for Paris in 1865, it becomes a performance tradition of its own.

timeline.label: Orson Welles directs the Federal Theatre Project’s Black-cast Macbeth
timeline.detail: Staged at the Lafayette Theatre in Harlem and relocated to a Caribbean island.

places.name: Inverness
places.note: Macbeth’s castle, where Duncan is murdered while a guest.

places.name: Forres
places.note: Duncan’s court, where Macbeth is thanked and Malcolm is named heir.

places.name: Dunsinane Hill
places.note: Macbeth’s fortress in the last act, and the hill Birnam wood must reach.

places.name: Birnam
places.note: The wood the soldiers cut for cover, about twelve miles from Dunsinane.

places.name: Iona
places.note: Colmekill, where Duncan’s body is carried for burial among his ancestors.

criticalViews.summary: In his note on the play Johnson praised the “solemnity, grandeur, and variety of its action” but found “no nice discriminations of character”: the events are so large that they decide what the characters do. He thought Lady Macbeth “merely detested”, and that Macbeth’s courage keeps some respect for him without making the reader sorry at his fall.

criticalViews.essay: On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth
criticalViews.summary: De Quincey asks why the knocking after Duncan’s murder is so disturbing. His answer is that while the murderers are alone the ordinary world is suspended. The knocking announces that it has come back, and the audience then feels how far outside it the murder took place.

Bradley stresses the darkness, storm and blood that fill the play. He reads Macbeth as a man of strong imagination whose conscience reaches him as terrifying images rather than as moral argument, and Lady Macbeth as someone whose will is stronger than her nature, so that it holds until the deed is done and then gives way.

criticalViews.work: How Many Children Had Lady Macbeth?
criticalViews.summary: Knights attacked criticism, Bradley’s above all, that treats Shakespeare’s characters as people with lives beyond the play. He read *Macbeth* as a dramatic poem organised by its imagery and its themes, such as the confusion of values in “Fair is foul” and the disorder that follows the murder of a king. The essay was published as a pamphlet and reprinted in his *Explorations* (1946).

criticalViews.essay: The Naked Babe and the Cloak of Manliness
criticalViews.summary: Taking up Caroline Spurgeon’s observation that Macbeth’s titles hang on him like borrowed clothes, Brooks follows a second set of images: babies, from the “naked new-born babe” of Macbeth’s soliloquy to the crowned child the witches show him. He argues that the babe stands for the future, which Macbeth tries and fails to control.

criticalViews.essay: “Born of Woman”: Fantasies of Maternal Power in Macbeth
criticalViews.summary: Adelman argues that the play is shaped by a fear of women’s power over men, seen in the witches and in Lady Macbeth’s call to the spirits to “unsex me here”. She reads the ending, where Macbeth is killed by a man “from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripp’d” and the women have vanished from the play, as a fantasy of escape from that power. A revised version is in her book *Suffocating Mothers* (1992).

Sinfield notes that the play condemns Macbeth’s violence while praising the violence done on behalf of Duncan and Malcolm, Macbeth’s own in the first act included. He connects this with the claim of James I’s state to be the only lawful user of violence, and asks whether the play supports that claim or shows how it works.
